title: Te Hiku Media's te reo Māori speech recognition reaches a reported 92% accuracy; archive transcription tests with the University of Auckland, RNZ and Ngā Taonga are under way
summary: Iwi broadcaster's ASR, trained on 310 hours of community recordings (86% accuracy, 2022), reported at 92% in 2024; archive tests announced in 2024 with results to come; no speaker outcome documented.
account: Te Hiku Media, a charitable iwi media and technology organization in Kaitaia, New Zealand, built its own te reo Māori automatic speech recognition. MIT Technology Review (22 April 2022) reported that a 2018 community competition collected '310 hours of speech-text pairs from some 200,000 recordings made by roughly 2,500 people' in ten days, from which, bootstrapping an open-source Mozilla model, 'Te Hiku created its very first te reo speech recognition model with 86% accuracy'; the tools are offered through the Papa Reo platform. NVIDIA's blog (16 January 2024) says the model 'transcribes te reo Māori with 92% accuracy' using the NeMo toolkit, and an RNZ release of 11 September 2024 quotes Te Hiku chief executive Peter-Lucas Jones in te reo giving the same 92% figure. The University of Auckland announced on 18 March 2024, the date used here, that its Archive of Māori and Pacific Sound is collaborating with Te Hiku Media to test the tool on archival recordings with different dialects, recording qualities and sung forms, comparing automatic output 'against human-generated ones', with results to be shared with the galleries, libraries, archives and museums sector; it says the tool 'is performing very well for their purposes' in Te Hiku's broadcasting arm. RNZ and Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision agreed in September 2024 to supply previously broadcast te reo recordings to train and review the tools. No fetched source reports a measured outcome for a speaker, learner or archive user; the accuracy figures originate with Te Hiku Media and NVIDIA.
purpose: Built to transcribe te reo Māori recordings so that archives and broadcasts become searchable and readable by learners, under Māori data-sovereignty rules; the transcription tests are that intended use.
system: Te Hiku Media te reo Māori automatic speech recognition and transcription tool (Papa Reo platform; trained with Mozilla DeepSpeech-era open-source tooling, later NVIDIA NeMo)
deployer: Te Hiku Media broadcasting arm; test partners Archive of Māori and Pacific Sound (University of Auckland), RNZ and Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision
taxonomy_note: Accessibility is the closest type: transcripts make te reo recordings usable by learners and archive users. General benefit with null depths because the fetched sources document capability (86% then 92% accuracy, as reported by the developer and relayed by NVIDIA and RNZ) and announced tests, not an attributable outcome; the University of Auckland test results had not been published in any fetched source.

ratings.reason: Te Hiku Media and its archive partners report the tool performs well for broadcasting and are testing it on archival material; no measured time saving or completed archive transcription is documented.
Benefits to te reo speakers and learners are the stated aim; no fetched source measures them.

ai_role.statement: The accuracy figures come from Te Hiku Media (86% reported by MIT Technology Review in 2022; 92% stated by NVIDIA, a tooling vendor, and by Te Hiku's chief executive through RNZ in 2024). The University of Auckland's independent test compares outputs against human transcripts with results to follow; no fetched source reports an outcome for any speaker, learner or archive beyond the developer's own broadcasting use.
